title: TankoVault Scan Pipeline
description: Everything between a scheduled scan and a user being told about a new chapter: scheduling, per-provider task throughput and backlog, where a slow run's wall clock actually went, outbound fetches and the throttling they earn, notification fan-out, AniList synchronisation, and the recommendation model built from the catalogue the rest of it fills. The backlog row needs `metrics.natsExporter.enabled` — NATS publishes no Prometheus exposition of its own, so those panels are empty rather than wrong without it.

panels.title: Scheduler leadership
panels.description: Exactly one control-plane replica should hold the lease. 0 means nothing is planning scan runs — a silent outage with every service up. More than 1 is split brain, usually clock skew.

panels.title: Scan runs planned
panels.description: `duplicate` climbing alongside a healthy `planned` rate is the fingerprint of two schedulers both believing they are leader.

panels.title: Scheduler sweep duration (p95)
panels.description: One sweep over every active provider. Queried directly rather than through a recording rule: it is a diagnostic for a wedged scheduler, not something alerted on.

panels.title: Duplicate sweep
panels.description: The maintenance pass that merges series the adapters registered twice. Its verdicts are the only visibility into it — `auto_merged` climbing steadily means a provider is producing near-duplicate listings, which is an adapter problem rather than an operational one.

panels.title: Scan tasks served per provider lane
panels.description: Tasks handed to a worker. A redelivered task counts again, so a failing lane can look busy — read this against the settlement panels below.

panels.title: Scan tasks served per tier
panels.description: Fast scans surface a new release; full scans rebuild the catalogue. Full flowing with fast at zero means the fast lanes did not open — strict priority makes queueing behind a full backlog impossible.

panels.title: Tasks served per provider, last hour
panels.description: One provider taking nearly everything is either the others having no work, or their lanes having failed to open.

panels.title: Task duration (p95) per tier
panels.description: Wall time for one scan task. Full-tier duration rising with a flat fetch latency points at the catalogue growing rather than at the provider slowing down.

panels.title: Providers in flight, and lanes with work
panels.description: Two reads on provider concurrency. `lanes (30m)` counts the providers served at least one task in the last 30 minutes — round-robin fairness predicts it tracks the number of providers with work, and one lane climbing alone is the signature of lanes that failed to open. `in flight (per worker)` is what a worker replica is executing right now; a worker runs at most one task per provider, so it is also the number of providers being crawled at this instant, capped per replica by `worker.max_concurrent_providers` (default 4). Pinned at the cap means the queue is the constraint; below the cap while the backlog row is non-empty means every remaining provider already has a task in flight, and more worker replicas would not help.

panels.title: Share of task time by stage
panels.description: Where a scan task's wall clock goes, as each stage's share of all stage time for that provider. Time in a `*_fetch` stage is the provider's; `series_ingest` is our own write into the catalogue, and a rising ingest share is a database problem wearing a scan's clothes. Read this only once the pace-wait share to the right is low — on a politeness-bound provider these shares describe what little time was left over.

panels.title: Stage duration (p95)
panels.description: The same split in absolute terms: how long one task spends in one stage. The share panel says which stage dominates, this one says whether the stage itself got slower or simply ran more often.

panels.title: Pace-wait share of task time
panels.description: The first number to read on a slow scan: the share of a task spent waiting for *permission to send* — the concurrency gate, the token rate, the crawl delay and any adaptive 429 penalty. Near 1 the scan is polite, not broken, and nothing in the code will speed it up: raise `politeness.rps` or lower `crawl_delay_ms` for that provider, or accept the duration. Near 0 with a long task duration means the time is in the requests or in the ingest, and the stage panels say which.

panels.title: Waiting for permission to send (p95)
panels.description: The same wait unscaled, at both layers that show it. `per task` is what one scan task accumulated across every request it made; `per request` is one request's wait, which climbs on its own when a provider starts answering 429/503 because the adaptive penalty widens that provider's spacing — a rise there with no configuration change is the throttle working rather than a fault.

panels.title: Scan queue depth per provider lane
panels.description: Undelivered tasks sitting in JetStream. Empty panel means the NATS exporter is not deployed — the broker publishes no Prometheus exposition of its own.

panels.title: Queue depth per tier
panels.description: A fast-tier backlog larger than the provider count is impossible by design: a fast run enqueues at most one task per provider.

panels.title: Redelivered tasks, and the notifier backlog
panels.description: Redelivery is bounded at three attempts, so a lane holding redelivered messages continuously is failing rather than hiccupping. The events queue is the notifier's, which acks only after fan-out — a hanging channel stalls everything behind it.

panels.title: Task outcomes
panels.description: Terminal states, counted once each — unlike the served counter, a task retried twice and then completed contributes one `completed` here, not three.

panels.title: Task failure ratio per lane
panels.description: `requeued` is excluded from the numerator: a requeue is the retry mechanism working, and a task that keeps being requeued is counted once when it finally settles as failed.

panels.title: Fetch rate by outcome
panels.description: A 4xx is usually a chapter that has been taken down and is normal; only `5xx` and `error` mean the provider is unusable right now.

panels.title: Fetch failure ratio
panels.description: Server faults and transport errors over all fetches. Every challenge-protected provider failing at once points at the solver, not at the sites.

panels.title: Fetch latency (p95)
panels.description: Excludes rate-limiter and backoff waiting, so this is the site's own response time.

panels.title: Backoff duty cycle
panels.description: Seconds of backoff accrued per second: 1.0 means one crawler is parked on this provider full time. Directly comparable against the worker replica count, so it needs no baseline to read.

panels.title: Backoff events
panels.description: How often a provider answered 429/503 and the crawler stood down. Rising here with a flat failure ratio is the throttle working as intended.

panels.title: Chapters discovered, last hour
panels.description: The output of the whole pipeline. Zero across every provider while tasks are being served means scans are running and finding nothing.

panels.title: Listing entries rejected
panels.description: The adapter refusing entries it cannot parse. Near 1.0 is what a provider redesign looks like from here: the fetch works, the page parses, no selector matches.

panels.title: Catalogue walks cut short
panels.description: Hitting the `max_catalog_pages` ceiling. Persistent truncation means the provider's catalogue is larger than the walk is allowed to cover, so the tail is never seen.

panels.title: Event processing failure ratio
panels.description: The notifier failing to process a chapter event at all, so not even the durable in-app row is written and the loss is permanent for those events.

panels.title: Deliveries by channel and outcome
panels.description: `skipped` is a channel a user has not configured, not a failure. A channel that hangs rather than fails shows up as a queue that stops draining, not here.

panels.title: Fan-out duration (p95) and live push failures
panels.description: Fan-out is what the notifier holds the message for; the SSE ratio is the api's end of the same path, where a failure costs the live toast but not the notification.

panels.title: Requests by operation and result
panels.description: `sync` is the only service that talks to AniList, and its latency is deliberately not part of that service's readiness — this is the only place a degrading AniList shows up.

panels.title: Rate-limited share
panels.description: The budget is per application token and shared by every user of this deployment, so restarting sync does not help — the pull interval or a burst of new connections does.

panels.title: Request duration (p95) by operation
panels.description: Includes the client's own paced wait, so this rises when the budget is being rationed as well as when AniList itself is slow.

panels.title: Series the model covers
panels.description: Rows the recommendation model holds, per table. Flat while the catalogue grows means builds are failing or no replica is holding scheduler leadership. Absent entirely means no build has ever completed — the state a fresh deployment is in until its first full build, during which every incremental build refuses to run and every shelf comes back empty.

panels.title: Model builds, last hour
panels.description: Series processed by a build, split by stage and result. `incremental` runs on a quarter-hourly cadence and touches only what changed; `full` is weekly by default and re-solves the projection over the whole catalogue. A `failed` line at all is `TankoVaultRecsysBuildFailing`.

panels.title: Build duration (p95)
panels.description: A full build re-counts the vocabulary and re-solves the projection from the whole catalogue and is expected in minutes; an incremental one is proportional to catalogue churn, not to catalogue size. An incremental duration tracking the full one means the incremental ceiling is binding.

panels.title: Items per served shelf
panels.description: The earliest symptom of a broken or unbuilt model, and the one invisible in request latency: an empty shelf is a `200` served faster than a full one. Read against the serve rate on the same panel — a mean near zero only means anything while shelves are actually being asked for.

panels.title: Shelf serve latency (p95)
panels.description: Split by how the shelf was produced. `cached` is a single row read; `computed` runs one approximate-nearest-neighbour search per seed, so its tail is where the seed count shows up rather than where the catalogue size does.
